title: Chemistry X · 2024 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Part II Chemistry. It contains official comments on candidates' responses to the 2024 SSC-II Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: Most candidates demonstrated a thorough understanding of specific concepts and constructed better responses. They excelled in areas such as identifying Le Chatelier's Principle and providing its basic definition, offering recommendations on government strategies to mitigate the environmental impact of excessive fuel consumption, and discussing industrial applications of common salt. Nevertheless, teachers should concentrate on: (1) Maintenance of clear division between designated sections of CRQs and ERQs, (2) Reason behind each factor affecting equilibrium, (3) Identification of functional groups in an organic compound, (4) Recognition of the importance of water for its occurrence and sustainable existence, and (5) Understanding of terminologies like common salt and the difference between industrial, domestic, commercial, and laboratory uses.

questions.questionText:
Consider the given reaction at equilibrium.
PCl3(g) + Cl2(g) ⇌ PCl5(g)   (ΔH = −124 kJ/mol)
a. With reference to the given chemical reaction, complete the table by writing the reason for each cause and effect.
   i. Increase in temperature shifts equilibrium towards left
   ii. Increase in pressure shifts equilibrium towards right
questions.sloText: Determine the effect of catalyst, temperature, pressure and concentration on a reversible reaction at equilibrium.
checkingHints: 1 mark for each correct reason (2 required):
i. The reaction is exothermic (ΔH is negative, heat is released in forward direction), so adding heat shifts the reaction in the reverse direction (left).
ii. There are fewer moles of gas on the product side (1 mole vs 2 moles on reactant side), so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the right to undo the stress.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates showed an ample understanding of macroscopic properties of reversible reactions. However, some candidates confused reversible and reverse reactions or repeated the prompt without explaining the enthalpy sign or gaseous mole ratio.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses correctly identified the given reaction as exothermic by highlighting the negative sign of ΔH (−124 kJ/mol), explaining that heat is released in the forward reaction so adding heat drives the reaction in the reverse direction (left). In part 'ii', better responses noted that the product side has fewer moles of gas (1 mole vs 2 moles), so increased pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles (right).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses repeated the cause-and-effect statement already printed in the table, or mistakenly labelled the reaction as endothermic and claimed pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with more moles or higher density.
suggestions: Train students to explicitly reference the sign of ΔH (negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic) when explaining temperature shifts, and to count gaseous moles on both sides when explaining pressure shifts.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. The reaction shifts towards the left on increasing temperature because it is an exothermic reaction having a negative enthalpy (ΔH) value.
ii. On increasing pressure, mass per unit volume is increased, so the equilibrium shifts towards the right (product side) having fewer number of moles of gas (1 mole vs 2 moles) to undo the stress imposed.

questions.questionText: Identify the principle applied to this chemical reaction. Support your identification with a suitable reason. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Determine the effect of catalyst, temperature, pressure and concentration on a reversible reaction at equilibrium.
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying Le Chatelier's principle.
1 mark for the correct reason (if an external stress such as temperature or pressure is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that undoes/nullifies the stress).
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed well on this question by clearly identifying Le Chatelier's Principle, though a few struggled with spelling or confused it with the Law of Mass Action.
questions.betterResponses: Candidates who provided better responses successfully identified Le Chatelier's Principle and explained that if an external stress (such as temperature or pressure) is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system moves in the direction that undoes or nullifies the applied stress to maintain equilibrium.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses misidentified the principle as the 'Law of mass action' or discussed reaction rate and Q_c vs K_c instead of Le Chatelier's principle of stress counteraction.
suggestions: Clearly distinguish the Law of Mass Action (which relates reaction rate to active masses and defines K_c) from Le Chatelier's Principle (which predicts the direction of equilibrium shift when external stress is applied).
questions.modelAnswer: Le Chatelier's principle is applied to this reaction because it states that if an external stress (such as temperature, pressure, or concentration change) is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that undoes/nullifies the stress imposed.

questions.questionText:
Given are three different compounds with four carbon atoms.
Compound I: Cyclobutane (C4H8)
Compound II: Butanoic acid (CH3–CH2–CH2–CO2H)
Compound III: 1-Butene (CH3–CH2–CH=CH2)
a. Identify compound II based on its functional group. (1 Mark)
b. Write any ONE similarity and ONE difference between compounds I and III. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Classify organic compounds into acyclic and cyclic compounds with examples; identify a molecule's functional group using structural formula and systematic names of compounds up to five carbon atoms.
checkingHints: a. 1 mark for the identification (Carboxylic acid / carboxyl group, Butanoic acid).
b. 1 mark for the similarity (both have the same molecular formula C4H8 / 4 carbons and 8 hydrogens).
c. 1 mark for the difference (Compound I is a closed-chain cyclic saturated hydrocarbon, whereas Compound III is an open-chain acyclic unsaturated alkene with a C=C double bond).
questions.overallPerformance: A significant number of candidates successfully depicted the similarities and differences between Compounds I and III, but many struggled to recognise the condensed carboxyl group (–CO2H) in Compound II.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly identified the functional group in part 'a' as a carboxylic acid (carboxyl group, –COOH / –CO2H) with the IUPAC name butanoic acid. In part 'b', they noted the shared molecular formula C4H8 as the similarity and contrasted closed-chain (cyclic) saturated structure I with open-chain (acyclic) unsaturated alkene structure III.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses misidentified the –CO2H group in Compound II as an aldehyde, alcohol, ketone, or ester. In part 'b', some gave generic statements about alkanes and alkenes without connecting them to the cyclic vs. acyclic structures shown.
suggestions: Familiarise students with all three standard notations for the carboxyl functional group: expanded –C(=O)–OH, condensed –COOH, and condensed –CO2H.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. The functional group present in Compound II is the carboxylic (carboxyl) group; the compound is Butanoic acid.
b. Similarity: Both Compound I and Compound III have the same molecular formula, C4H8.
   Difference: Compound I is a closed-chain (cyclic) saturated hydrocarbon, whereas Compound III is an open-chain (acyclic) unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond.

questions.questionText:
Two beakers, labelled as A and B, contain two different carbohydrates. The carbohydrate in beaker A dissolves only in hot water while the carbohydrate in beaker B easily dissolves in cold water.
a. Which beaker contains sugar and which one has starch? (1 Mark)
b. Why the carbohydrate in beaker A dissolves in hot water only? (1 Mark)
c. Name the simplest form of carbohydrates. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Compare the solubility of starch and glucose in water.
checkingHints: a. 1 mark for correct identification (Beaker A = Starch, Beaker B = Sugar).
b. 1 mark for the correct reason (Starch is a complex polysaccharide with many glycosidic linkages requiring hot water to break down and dissolve).
c. 1 mark for naming the simplest form of carbohydrate (Monosaccharides / glucose).
questions.overallPerformance: Overall performance was satisfactory, though candidates who swapped Beakers A and B in part 'a' lost the thread of reasoning in part 'b'.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'a', better responses accurately identified Starch in Beaker A and Sugar in Beaker B. In part 'b', they explained that starch is a macromolecular polysaccharide containing numerous glycosidic linkages (with linear amylose and branched amylopectin) that requires hot water to dissolve. In part 'c', they named monosaccharides (such as glucose or fructose) as the simplest form of carbohydrates.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses swapped the beakers (claiming Beaker A had sugar and Beaker B had starch) and wrote that 'sugar freezes in cold water', or listed all three classes of carbohydrates in part 'c' instead of naming the simplest form.
suggestions: Demonstrate the solubility difference between table sugar/glucose and cornstarch in cold vs. hot water in the classroom.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Beaker A – Starch; Beaker B – Sugar.
b. Beaker A dissolves in hot water only because starch is a complex polysaccharide with many glycosidic linkages that require heat energy (hot water) to break down and dissolve.
c. Monosaccharides.

questions.questionText: Write any THREE features of water with reference to its occurrence on the Earth. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the occurrence of water in the environment.
checkingHints: 1 mark for writing each feature regarding water's occurrence on Earth (any 3 required): ~97% in oceans, ~2.1% in glaciers/ice caps, ~0.6% groundwater, only ~0.2% potable freshwater, covers ~71% of Earth's surface, exists in all three physical states (solid, liquid, gas).
questions.overallPerformance: Performance was moderate. Better responses cited the percentage distribution of Earth's water across oceans, glaciers, groundwater, and atmospheric vapour, whereas weaker responses wrote physical/chemical properties of water (like pH or litmus tests) instead of its environmental occurrence.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses stated that ~97% of Earth's water is in the oceans, the remaining water is distributed across glaciers/ice caps (~2.1%), groundwater (~0.6%), and atmospheric water vapour, only ~0.2% is potable freshwater because ocean water has a high percentage of dissolved salts, and water coexists naturally in all three states of matter (solid, liquid, and gas).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses wrote unrelated properties such as 'it is neutral on pH scale', 'it turns red litmus paper to blue', hard vs. soft water, or domestic uses like washing clothes.
suggestions: Draw attention to the qualifying phrase 'with reference to its occurrence on the Earth' so students provide geographical/environmental distribution data rather than laboratory physical properties.
questions.currentTopic: Environmental Chemistry II: Occurrence of Water
questions.modelAnswer:
1. About 97% of total water on Earth is in the oceans as salty water.
2. The rest of the water on Earth is present in the form of glaciers and ice caps (~2.1%), groundwater (~0.6%), and water vapours in the atmosphere.
3. Only about 0.2% of water on Earth is potable freshwater because ocean water contains a high percentage of dissolved salts.

questions.questionText:
i. Write any FOUR industrial uses of common salt. (4 Marks)
ii. Give any ONE example of each of the following types of salt. (2 Marks)
   I. Mixed salt
   II. Double salt
questions.sloText: Discuss the uses of salts in daily life and industries; exemplify the different types of salts (acidic, basic, normal, double, mixed and complex).
checkingHints: i. 1 mark for writing each industrial use of common salt (NaCl) (any 4 required).
ii.I. 1 mark for any 1 example of mixed salt (e.g. Bleaching powder, Ca(OCl)Cl).
ii.II. 1 mark for any 1 example of double salt (e.g. Potash alum, K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O).
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates generally demonstrated a solid grasp of salt classification, though some confused 'common salt' (specifically NaCl) with salts in general or swapped mixed and double salt examples.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses in part 'i' listed industrial uses of NaCl: raw material (brine) in the Solvay process to manufacture Na2CO3 and NaHCO3, regenerating sodium zeolite resins in industrial water softeners, food preservation, and manufacturing caustic soda, chlorine, plastics, and glass. In part 'ii', they gave bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl as a mixed salt and potash alum K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O as a double salt.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses listed uses of other salts (like potash alum or CaCl2) instead of common salt (NaCl), mentioned domestic uses (home cooking or road de-icing), and swapped the examples of mixed salt and double salt in part 'ii'.
suggestions: Clarify that 'common salt' specifically refers to Sodium Chloride (NaCl) and distinguish industrial manufacturing uses from domestic household uses.
questions.currentTopic: Acids, Bases and Salts (Types & Uses of Salts)
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Industrial Uses of Common Salt (NaCl):
1. Concentrated NaCl (brine) is used in the Solvay process for the industrial manufacture of baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3).
2. NaCl is used commercially to regenerate sodium zeolite resins used to remove permanent hardness of water.
3. Used in the food industry to flavour and preserve food (fish, meat, pickles).
4. Used in the manufacture of caustic soda (NaOH), chlorine gas, soaps, plastics, and glass.
ii.I. Mixed Salt: Bleaching powder, Ca(OCl)Cl.
ii.II. Double Salt: Potash alum, K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O.

questions.questionText:
Hydrocarbons are used as feedstock (raw material) in many industrial processes. A few examples of hydrocarbon feeds are ethylene and acetylene.
i. Draw the structure for ethylene and acetylene. (2 Marks)
ii. Describe the use of the following hydrocarbons in the manufacturing of their respective polymer and any TWO durable articles in the mentioned industries. (4 Marks)
   I. Ethylene in plastic industry
   II. Acetylene in rubber industry
questions.sloText: Explain the use of hydrocarbons as: a. fuel b. feedstock in industry.
checkingHints: i. 1 mark for structure of ethylene (H2C=CH2) + 1 mark for structure of acetylene (H–C≡C–H).
ii.I. Ethylene in plastic industry: 1 mark for making polyethene polymer + 1 mark for any TWO durable plastic articles (plastic bags, plates, PVC pipes, toys).
ii.II. Acetylene in rubber industry: 1 mark for making butadiene/neoprene synthetic rubber + 1 mark for any TWO durable rubber articles (tyres, rubber footwear/slippers, gloves).
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates attempted this question and performed well, though a common error was failing to name butadiene/neoprene rubber as the polymer derived from acetylene.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses drew accurate Lewis/structural formulas for ethylene (H2C=CH2) and acetylene (H–C≡C–H). In part 'ii', they described ethylene being polymerised into polyethene to make plastic shoppers, plates, crockery, and pipes, and acetylene being used to make butadiene synthetic rubber for manufacturing tyres and rubber footwear (slippers).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses attached –OH groups to ethylene/acetylene in part 'i', omitted the specific polymer names in part 'ii', or listed only one article instead of two.
suggestions: Create a summary table linking each petrochemical monomer (ethylene, propylene, acetylene) to its industrial polymer (polyethene, polypropylene, polybutadiene/neoprene rubber) and end-use consumer products.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Ethylene (C2H4): H2C=CH2; Acetylene (C2H2): H–C≡C–H.
ii.I. In the plastic industry, ethylene is used to make polyethene (and PVC), which is moulded into durable articles such as plastic shopping bags, plates/crockery, toys, and PVC pipes.
ii.II. In the rubber industry, acetylene is used to make butadiene (and neoprene) synthetic rubber, which is used to manufacture durable articles such as automobile tyres and rubber footwear (slippers/shoes).

questions.questionText:
In Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad, the use of private vehicles has increased drastically due to insufficient public transport. Higher usage of private vehicles has increased fuel consumption in these cities.
i. Describe any THREE effects of increased fuel consumption on the environment. (3 Marks)
ii. With reference to the effects described in part i, suggest any THREE ways to minimise them at the government level. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe sources and effects of air pollutants; recommend strategies that the governments adopt to control air pollution.
checkingHints: i. 1 mark for describing each environmental effect (any 3 required: global warming from CO2, acid rain from NOx/SO2, respiratory diseases/poor AQI from toxic exhaust gases).
ii. 1 mark for mentioning each government-level suggestion (any 3 required: promote public transport, mandate catalytic converters, promote afforestation, transition to electric/solar/wind energy).
questions.overallPerformance: Many candidates demonstrated a strong understanding of vehicular air pollution and proposed practical government-level remedies.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses explained that increased fuel combustion releases CO and CO2 (trapping IR radiation and causing global warming, glacier melting, and flooding), releases nitrogen/sulphur oxides that cause acid rain, and releases toxic smoke/particulates that cause respiratory problems in asthmatic patients. In part 'ii', they recommended government actions: mandating catalytic converters in vehicles, expanding public transport (metro/electric trains), planting trees (afforestation), and shifting to solar/wind/hydro energy and electric vehicles.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses focused on economic issues ('high petrol prices, petrol shortages') or noise pollution rather than chemical environmental effects, and gave vague personal advice rather than government policies.
suggestions: Encourage students to connect each specific tailpipe pollutant (CO2, CO, NOx, SO2) to its corresponding atmospheric impact (global warming, asphyxiation/smog, acid rain) and targeted government policy.
questions.currentTopic: Environmental Chemistry I: Air Pollution & Control Strategies
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Effects of Increased Fuel Consumption:
1. Releases CO2 gas which traps infrared (IR) radiation, leading to global warming and climate change.
2. Releases oxides of nitrogen and sulphur which form nitric and sulphuric acids, causing acid rain.
3. Releases toxic smoke and CO gas, degrading air quality and causing respiratory problems (especially for asthmatic people).
ii. Government-Level Strategies:
1. Ensure mandatory installation of catalytic converters in vehicles to convert NOx and CO into N2 and CO2.
2. Expand quality public transport (metro buses, electric trains) and encourage electric vehicles to reduce private fuel use.
3. Launch large-scale tree plantation (afforestation) drives and replace thermal coal/oil power with hydro, wind, and solar energy.

questions.questionText:
Diesel and petrol are liquid fuels that are extracted from petroleum. Diesel is used in ships while petrol is utilised as fuel for internal combustion engines of cars.
i. Name and describe the process through which diesel and petrol are obtained from petroleum. (2 Marks)
ii. Describe which type of hydrocarbons diesel and petrol are. With reference to their boiling points, mention their point of collection from the apparatus. (4 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the fractional distillation of petroleum.
checkingHints: i. 1 mark for naming Fractional Distillation + 1 mark for describing separation of crude oil into fractions based on boiling points at ~400°C.

ii. 1 mark for describing diesel fraction (C13–C15, BP 250–350°C) + 1 mark for lower end of fractionating column + 1 mark for describing petrol fraction (C7–C10, BP 80–170°C) + 1 mark for upper end of fractionating column.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates who chose 6b generally performed satisfactorily, though some confused fractional distillation of crude oil with mining/drilling petroleum from rock or destructive distillation of coal.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses named Fractional Distillation and defined it as separating crude oil heated to 400°C in a distillation tower into fractions according to their boiling points. In part 'ii', they stated that diesel consists of C13–C15 hydrocarbons (more viscous, less flammable, higher boiling point 250–350°C) collected at the lower end (5th outlet) of the tower, while petrol (gasoline) consists of C7–C10 hydrocarbons (less viscous, more flammable, lower boiling point 80–170°C) collected near the upper end (3rd outlet) of the tower.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses confused fractional distillation with 'destructive distillation of coal' or 'extracting rock oil from underground', failed to specify carbon chain lengths and boiling ranges, or wrote about fuel taxes and IMF loans.
suggestions: Use a labelled diagram of a petroleum fractionating tower showing carbon chain length, boiling range (°C), condensation height (top vs. bottom), and uses for all six fractions.
questions.currentTopic: Chemical Industries & Fractional Distillation of Petroleum
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Fractional Distillation: The separation of crude oil into various fractions according to their boiling points by heating crude oil up to 400°C in a fractionating tower.
ii. Diesel vs. Petrol:
- Diesel: Consists of C13 to C15 hydrocarbons (more viscous, less flammable) with a higher boiling point of 250°C–350°C, collected at the lower end (5th point) of the fractionating tower.
- Petrol (Gasoline): Consists of C7 to C10 hydrocarbons (less viscous, more flammable) with a lower boiling point of 80°C–170°C, collected near the upper end (3rd point) of the fractionating tower.
